description: In the Alto Valle of Río Negro, vegetable plots are irrigated from canals that close for winter, so the plot often sits bare until the next spring crop. I'm building Umbral to help growers use that gap without wasting seed, fuel and work. It compares leaving the plot as it is with a grass cover and a legume cover: whether the dates fit the last canal turns, early cold nights (NASA POWER), real parcels in a past season (NASA HLS), and what each cover is for. The grower decides.
summary:
Umbral is a decision-support web app for growers in the Alto Valle of Rio Negro, Argentina, where irrigation canals close for winter. Between two annual crops the plot often sits bare; in orchards the interrow, and in strawberry beds the paths, are managed around a crop that stays. Umbral helps a grower explore a service crop for that time and space before investing seed, fuel and work, and shows honestly what NASA data can and cannot say about it.

The grower sets the production system (annual rotation, permanent orchard or beds), the commercial crops, the goal, the free dates and the canal water. Umbral evaluates nine candidate cover crops, four established and five experimental, compares their benefit, trade-off and evidence, and lists every check to settle before sowing. NASA HLS shows what was green on real dates over four study parcels near General Roca, NASA EMIT estimates green plants, dry material and bare soil, and NASA POWER gives 45 years of cold-night and rain history for the planned window. The rules are documented and tested; no yield, money or nitrogen amount is invented, and local agronomic validation is still pending.
details:
Live app: https://umbral-altovalle.vercel.app

Code (public repository, MIT): https://github.com/JuliaGastellu/umbral

Demo video (30 s): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Gq1jrciXOgWmRvZgk5VZSNhJrYvKjcgw/view?usp=sharing

The problem. In the Alto Valle of Rio Negro, Argentina, farms are irrigated from canals that close for winter, around late April, and reopen in August. Between two annual crops the plot often sits bare; in orchards the interrow, and in strawberry beds the paths, are managed around a crop that stays. A service crop could protect that soil, but sowing it costs seed, fuel, work and water the grower may not have. I built Umbral (one-person team, General Roca) to help growers explore that decision before investing, and to show honestly what NASA data can and cannot say about it.

How it works. The page is one journey. I start on a map of the public provincial parcel layer around General Roca with four study examples; only those four parcels have satellite readings, and the app says so. Four NASA layers each answer one question: what was green on a real 2024 date (HLS, 30 m), how the ground divided into green plants, dry material and bare soil (EMIT, the four examples together), and how often the planned window had enough days before a cold night in 45 years (POWER). Then the grower sets the management conditions: production system (annual rotation, permanent orchard or beds), commercial crops, goal, dates and canal water. Umbral evaluates nine candidates, four established and five experimental, shows up to three side by side with their benefit, trade-off and evidence, and lets the grower select one. That option drives the calendar, the cold-night question, the date comparison, the nitrogen-process chain, saving and export (JSON and Markdown), and every check to settle before sowing is listed at once. Leaving the ground as it is stays a valid baseline.

Rules and honesty. The rules are documented and tested, with no score. A cover whose dates or system do not fit cannot be selected; a weaker match for the goal stays selectable with that limit shown. Missing inputs, water that may not reach the cover area, and reported waterlogging or salinity make an option conditional without changing its dates. No money, yield or nitrogen amount is computed. A station check shows that the regional NASA POWER record places cold nights later than the nearest station (Neuquen airport), and the app says so next to its climate readings. Agronomic validation with local growers is still pending.

Impact. Umbral turns a generic rule such as "sow vetch 30-45 days before a killing frost" into how many days there actually were in each of 45 years for this place, and connects satellite observations with the grower's own calendar, water and space. The goal is fewer wasted sowings, more living soil between crops, and a plan the grower can take to the irrigation consortium or an agronomist.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Vitest, Leaflet; Python (rasterio, earthaccess, shapely, pyproj, numpy, Pillow) for data processing; a read-only Cloudflare Workers API; Vercel hosting; Playwright and axe-core for browser and accessibility checks.

AI disclosure. The Umbral logo is AI-generated and carries a visible "Logo: AI-generated" mark in the app. I used AI assistants (large language models) to search literature, write and review code, run browser checks, draft documentation, and edit the demo video from my own screen recording and voice. I defined the problem, chose the data, assumptions and scope, and checked outputs against the cited sources. NASA imagery and charts are data, not generated images; no NASA logo or identifier was generated or altered.
